> Okay.  I took the try-the-300-BAUD-archiving-tools plunge today.  I setup my Astrocade, wrote a short two-line program and was able to save it in 300-BAUD format and get it back into the Astrocade (after some data manipulation using the PC).  First off, WAV2WAV worked fine for me.  It seems the simplest way to go.  Is there any reason that I should NOT use it?
>

wav2wav is definitely a handy program, and I like that it keeps the timing of the original recording.  You will need to use wav2raw, or KCS, if you want to get a binary dump.  Even if I use wav2wav, I generally get a binary (.prg) file separately.  With this, you can use prg2txt, and get the source code right on your PC.  It is essential to get a .prg file if you intend to do any corrections to the program on the PC.  For example, I might get a .prg file, transform it to an editable source listing with prg2txt -e, correct an error in the source, get a new .prg file with txt2prg, then convert the .prg file back into a .wav file that can be loaded onto the system.  (Yes, this can get a little convoluted.)

>
Also, I thought that there were some Astrocade-type docs for KCSWIN, but I couldn't find anything written by Paul.
>

Ronaldo put a bit of information into a readme with his programs, but I don't know of any complete documentation.  Here's the main things you need to know.

KCS is not as user-friendly as the Casio utilities, and isn't able to preserve timing in recordings.  However, I've often found it to give better results on difficult recordings.  As with the Casio utilities, results may be improved by first applying a 2400Hz high-pass filter to the recording.

.wav files input into KCS must be 22050Hz, 8 bit mono.  8 bit mono is an obsolete format that isn't supported by all programs.  Audacity can read these files, but won't save as 8 bit.  One program that does save as 8 bit is Goldwave (http://www.goldwave.com/).

To convert a recording into a .prg file, use:

KCSWIN.exe input.wav output.prg

KCS will stop on certain errors.  To continue through the recording regardless, use:

KCSWIN.exe -Y  input.wav output.prg

To convert a .prg file back into a clean, highly compressible .wav file, use something like:

KCSWIN.EXE -M -L3 -P50 INPUT.PRG OUTPUT.WAV

-M is to make the wavefile.  -L3 adds a 3 second leader to the recording.  -P50 adds a 50ms delay between each character.  Without this delay, some characters will get skipped when loading the recording.  For most programs, I've found a 35ms delay to be adequate, but occasionally a little longer is necessary.

Astrology:  It's not incorrect or anything, but I don't think the "(although it
made it into a few of the vaporware ads)" comment is really necessary now that I name the ad and quote its description.

Life:  I guess this gets into how we distinguish releases from prototypes.  By my criteria, if an independent game author sells a small number of cartridges (at shows, through a newsletter, etc.), then that is a commercial release.  We also have Mazeman under released carts, for example.  Discuss.

Sea Wolf / Bombardier:  From change log--"Removed suggestion that the name "Missile" in "Sea Wolf / Missile" was replaced
   by Bombardier due to problems with Atari.  The "Missile" name continued to be
   used on Astrovision packaging, and the game was based on "Missile X / Guided
   Missile" by Taito / Midway."

9800:
Just a couple brief thoughts, since you asked...

On Wed, 1/5/11, Adam Trionfo <ballyalley@hotmail.com> wrote:
> If someone could point me to a cut and dry definition of a
> "released" game versus a prototype or a homebrew, then please
> do.  I'm not going to be a stickler here.  I have no intention
> to go changing the FAQ and moving titles all around... but I'm
> curious.  What do other people think entails a released game?

There is no cut and dry, but I tend to think of it in terms of
production...  If a company, or even an individual, produces a
game for sale, think of taxes -- if the company or individual
has a Tax ID (or whatever it's called), then it's a production
game in some sense; but if the Tax ID is just the guy's SSN, or
he doesn't charge tax, well, that starts to smack of a homebrew.

And think of production methodology...  If someone paid to have
cart shells made, labels printed and ROMs burnt, it's not a
prototype, even if it never made it to stores.  But if someone
is reusing shells, making their own labels, and using EPROMs,
it's either a prototype or a homebrew.

Of course, there's line-blurring even if you think of it as the
above.  The "problem" is that production costs have come down
enough that "homebrews" CAN rival "releases", which wasn't true
for the most part in the 80s, and even early 90s.

> Paul Thacker wrote:
>> By my criteria, if an independent game author sells a small
>> number of cartridges (at shows, through a newsletter, etc.),
>> then that is a commercial release.

> It seems that normally any release is considered homebrew after
> the first-party stops supporting the platform.

I wouldn't go that far (sometimes third-party companies will
continue to produce games even after the first-party stops), but
it's generally fair to state it that way.  But you could still
have actually "production releases" well after a system's life
that wouldn't be homebrews exactly.

As an example, consider the Dreamcast.  The system does still get
the occasional release with Sega's blessing; it also gets the
occasional "hobbyist" release but with production GD-ROMs and
packaging...  The former are definitely NOT homebrews, and the
latter, while getting closer, still aren't, really.  But if someone
coded a new game and sold it on CDRs with ink-jet printed tray
cards and labels, well that WOULD be a homebrew, no matter where
he sold them, IMO.

The &(192)=0 is only needed on a Viper system to turn off the soft write protect.

That is, even though the AUTO/WR - PROG/WR switch is in the PROG/WR the Viper still protects righting to the first 8K unless you &(192)=0.
&(192)=255 turns it on again.

9872:
I picked up two of the Interlibrary Loan books from the library this afternoon and I've already found one tantalizing tid-bit in the book "Inside Electronic Game Design" by Arnie Katz and Laura Yates.  Paul's list rated this book "very interesting" because, as Paul says, "it appears to have a section analyzing why the system didn't have a wide success."  Paul is pretty-much right.  There is a very short section, perhaps not analyzing, but at least WONDERING "what if" the Bally Arcade had succeeded instead of the Atari 2600.  Here's the meat of the matter:


     "Provocative "what if" scenarios about the Channel F [a system that is mentioned earlier in the book] are scarce because Channel F was just too primitive.  Had is somehow succeeded against all reason, Channel F's shortcoming might have blunted the first video game boom and set the technological timetable back a half decade."
     "If the Bally Arcade had caught the public's interest, the US game business might be more like the British counterpart.  In the United Kingdom, small computers fill the niche occupied by cartridge consoles in the United States.  Instead of closed boxes like the Atari 2600, young Britons bought fully programmable computers.  While America's youth preferred Pac-Man strategies, British youngsters dabbled in programming their tiny machines.  That's party why there are more game software programmers per capita in the United Kingdom than in the United States."
     "Bally actively encouraged customers to try coding their own stuff.  Widespread popularity for the Professional Arcade could have rewritten the subsequent course of game design history.  It might have ushered in an era of do-it-yourself video game design.  The shareware boom of the 1980s could have started a decade earlier."


At first glance this might seem like it DID happen.  After all, there were the Apple II, Commodore 64 and Atari computers that allowed people to program them and bedroom coders DID arise (but not to the extent that it did in the U.K.).  Based on earlier comments in the book it's quite clear that the author is referring to cartridge-based systems like the 2600.  Think of it this way.  If the Atari 2600 came with a proper BASIC cartridge for $30 or $40 that allowed the ability to save/load programs from tape and, say, 4K of RAM, (all making it sorta-kinda similar to Bally BASIC) then this might be a similar statement.  The Astrocade had a few newsletters, but in the UK, even computers that sold far less than the Bally's 300,000 units sold had full-fledged magazines that lasted, in some cases, a decade.

It is difficult to play "what if," but I like that this question was proposed in 1996 in a book by Arnie Katz, a respected writer in the videogame business (some might call him a legend).  This isn't just a topic that just popped-up on a forum asked by some Astrocade "fan boy."  This is an idea put forth by someone that knew the industry well.  An insider that understood the videogame business at time of the original Bally Arcade era.  If Arnie thought that this "what if" could have caused a change in the way the video game design industry grew up in the United States (had things been just right), then it also makes me wonder what might have happened too.

Perhaps all it would have taken for the Bally Arcade to have made it was for those first initial units not to have had an overheating problem.  Maybe then, the console would have shown brighter.  We'll never know... but it's an interesting thought.

Could the success of the Bally Arcade have changed the console industry?  For those that understand a bit about the video game business in Britain in the 1980's, could the Bally really have done anything like Arnie suggests if the console had been a success?  Perhaps not selling as well as a first-tier system like the Atari 2600, but one that sold ten-times better, like the Intellivision at three million units.

What do YOU think would have happened if the Bally Arcade sold well?  Could things really HAVE BEEN DIFFERENT?

9877:
I think I know your problem. When you input into a Blue Ram unit through it's
input jack, you are using the Blue Ram's input circuit with the INS8154 and it's
own 2 transistor amplifier/ wave conditioner. This circuitry it greatly improved
over the AstroBasic's 2000 interface circuit. Astro has been known for it's
persnickety inputting. many people have mixed feelings about using the AB
because of this. It just isn't as good as Blue Ram's circuit. You may need to
adjust you tape player's volume. AB also is more finicky about CD or other input
sources. You may just be on the threshold of where the AB works, and when it
gets to a spot that is too weak or strong for it, it hiccups, thus giving you
garbage on the screen. Once the screen shown garbage on it, even if it is only
one or 2 pixels, astro rejects all after that because it can't sync up. Try a
different AB cart or change your input volume slightly up or down. as far as
procedure, you are doing it right.

Ken

9881:
One other thing to consider is the machine that created the tape. Mike Peace
used an industrial copying machine, is his information was put on the tape at a
very high volume and quality. He used fairly high quality tape.
Recording from another recorder may not be as strong. The oxide on the tape may
not be as good. The age of the recording may also play a part. Some tapes
"bleed-through" after a long time, causing part of the recording to work it's
way to another winding. This was heard in the 60's and 70's on some 45 RPM
records. They used to call it pre-echo. You would start to hear the beginning of
the song quietly before it actually started up at the desired volume. The same
thing happens with most tapes. The Metal Oxide were better tapes, but they were
costly.
The other factor that effected pre-echo was the thickness of the cellulose
itself. The thinner, the more pre-echo. You may not be able to hear it on a 2000
baud tape, but it would definitely effect where ever it was on the tape.
Any questions?
Ken

9889:
"Inside Electronic Game Design"

By Arnie Katz with Laurie Yates

Copyright 1996

 

Bally/Astrocade-related excerpt from pages 12-16

 

 

The "Rice Try" Programmables

 

To the untrained eye, video game technology inched ahead
at a glacial pace during the first half of the seventies.  Behind the scenes, developments unfolded with
the suddenness of a mid-winter blizzard. 
Development of more powerful microprocessors and more efficient memory
storage units gave pioneering electronic gamemakers the tools they needed.

 

Everyone in the industry could see that hardwired games
were a dead end.  A cartridge system
boasted more flexibility at a lower retail price.  Consumers might be willing to buy one Pong
machine, but they would never buy a new machine every time they wanted a
different game.  The beauty of a
cartridge system is that consumers buy the hardware once, instead of purchasing
it anew for each game.  Though the
Odyssey's programmability was a wonderful feature, the unit itself didn't have
the graphics or data-crunching power to do much with it.  In this one respect did single console games
like Pong have an advantage.  But
hardware engineers believed they knew the answer: Put the operating system and
other permanent code into the console and put only the specific instructions
for the game in the plug-in cartridge.

 

RCA's programmable console reached market first, around
1975, but it made no dent. 
Black-and-white graphics and a collection of games little better than
Pong kept the RCA Studio from developing a following.

 

Fairchild's Channel F, which made its debut in 1976, had
improved color graphics and smaller controllers, but their games were also not
very good.  The company wasn't very
experienced with this sort of entertainment, so Channel F, too, couldn't
penetrate the market to any great extent.

 

The Bally Professional Arcade debuted in mid-1977.  It could have changed electronic game design
history, but it didn't.  Its high price
($299 retail) and daunting promotional rhetoric prevented mass market
sales.  Many saw it as a junior computer,
not a high-voltage video game machine, and the public wasn't yet ready for that
leap.

 

This machine, conceived by the same company that earlier
disdained video coin-ops, was utterly different than the ones that ultimately
succeeded with the public: the Atari Video Computer System (VCS) and Magnavox's
Odyssey2.  The VCS, the most popular
machine, was a black box like the Nintendo Entertainment System or Sega
Genesis-- with the innards of its console off-limits to the user-- but the
Bally system let the average person actually program his or her own video game
designs.  Its console incorporated a calculator-style
keyboard, 8K of memory, and ports for up to four controllers.  These were a story in themselves, combining
joystick and paddle functions in one compact unit.

 

Bally's pride and joy was a cartridge that taught owners
how to program in BASIC, a "plain English" coding system popular in
the late 1970s and 1980s.  Programs could
be stored on tape cassettes and transferred to the Pro Arcade.

 

The system's documentation and advertising spoke
confidently of how Professional Arcade owners would advance from playing
prepared software to creating their own.  It was no idle dream.  User groups formed around the unit generated
many programs, including games, until Bally stopped supporting its stillborn
progeny.  (Astrovision bought the project
and relaunched it in 1981, but without success.)

 

The Bally Professional Arcade had four resident software
titles: a calculator, a drawing program, and two games.  Gunfight made excellent use of the unit's
controllers.  The one- or two-player
side-perspective shoot-out armed buckaroos with six shots each.  The gamer moved the gunfighter in a limited
area with the stick, aimed with the paddle, and fired by pressing a button.

 

Checkmate, the other game, was a one- to four-player
kinetic strategy contest with the same play-mechanic as Atari's later Surround.
 The player guides a constantly
elongating line so that the head didn't intersect any other line, on-screen
obstacle, or the playfield boundary.

 

These games set the style for the system's software
library: streamlined, action-oriented play-mechanics; a dash of strategy; and
colorful but simple graphics with no playfield background detail.  In short, these games were fun to play without
being so complex that smart Bally Professional Arcade users couldn't imagine
programming something as good or better.

 

 

The Road Not Taken

 

The Atari 2600 and the Magnavox Odyssey 2 rocked home
entertainment in 1978.  Their instant
retail success launched video gaming's "golden age" and did much to
shape the game design environment for years to come.

 

Could the Bally Professional Arcade, or even the
Fairchild Channel F, have cracked through eventually?  It's not likely, considering their
deficiencies.  Yet it could have
happened.  And had one of those stillborn
platforms overcome its handicaps, it would have profoundly affected the role of
the game designer, since dramatically altering hardware capabilities radically
changes the design job.  What a
difference that might have made to electronic entertainment in general, and
game designing in particular.

 

Provocative "what if ?" scenarios about the
Channel F are scarce because Channel F was just too primitive.  Had it somehow succeeded against all reason,
Channel F's shortcomings might have blunted the first video game boom and set
the technological time-table back a half decade or so.

 

The Bally Arcade is another, more tantalizing question.  Better marketing and merchandising, plus a
lower price, could have turned this gaming computer into a hit.

 

If the Bally Arcade had caught the public's interest, the
US
game business might be more like its British counterpart.  In the United
 Kingdom, small computers filled the niche occupied by
cartridge consoles in the United
  States.  Instead of closed boxes like the Atari 2600,
young Britons bought fully programmable computers.  While America's youth perfected Pac-Man
strategies, British youngsters dabbled in programming their tiny machines.  That's partly why there are more game software
programmers per capita in the United Kingdom
than in the United States.

 

Bally actively encouraged customers to try coding their
own stuff.  Widespread popularity for the
Professional Arcade could have rewritten the subsequent course of game design
history.  It might have ushered in an era
of do-it-yourself video game design.  The
shareware boom of the late 1980s could have started a decade earlier.

"Creative Computer Graphics"
By Annabel Jankel and Rocky Morton
Copyright 1984


Bally/Astrocade-Related Excerpt from page 84 of "Creative Computer Graphics."  There is artwork created in ZGRASS that accompanies this excerpt.  Although the reference to the Astrocade is really through ZGRASS here (and is quite brief, over all), I'm quite glad that Paul pointed this out, as it will soon add two more ZGRASS pictures to BallyAlley.com.  Also, as I've already said, I liked this book enough that I went ahead and ordered a used copy.  Here is the excerpt:


Among the programming languages which have attracted significant interest among artists are Kenneth Knowlton's BEFLIX for mosaics, John Whitney Jr's user program at UCLA and especially the GRASS and ZGRASS languages developed by Tom De Fanti in Chicago.  De Fanti has been the most energetic promoter of the use of computer graphics by artists; he turned to an early video games system, the Bally Arcade, to make cheap computer images in the late 1970s.  Artists working with him, such as Frank Dietrich, did the same and a community of artists developed in Chicago using the Bally system and a dialect of the BASIC language.  Dietrich's and Zsuzsa Molnar's work at first resembled Knowlton's BEFLIX patterns but were extended to other low-resolution styles by S. Wenegersh and others.

From there De Fanti advanced to using a computer at Illinois University and his team developed the GRASS system.  Images generated by the mainframe are displayed on the screen and filmed with a videocamera.  The signal is transmitted to an analogue image processor and displayed again.  De Fanti's collegue Don Sandin designed this processor to make real time interactive graphics flexible and accessible on low-cost equipment.  The work possible on this system is extremely varied, lending itself to abstract images with woven texture and shimmering ripples of colour.

ZGRASS, developed purely for graphics, is based on a simple microprocessor system and an ordinary television display.  It is very easy to learn but creates complex images as in Snake 1982 produced by Dietrich and Molnar, who have been collaborating in video, computer and performance art for several years.  In 1983 Dietrich abandoned ZGRASS and exhibited Softy 3, a new departure for him in the smoothness of its surfaces and the sense of depth.  This was produced on a VAX 11 /750 mainframe with software written in the Fortran language by the artist and David Coons.

At the present state of technology it would be unlikely that Snake 1982 and Softy 3 would be produced on the same system.  Each combination of hardware and software provides opportunities and constraints, which inevitably means that there are similarities between the creation of different artists on the same system, but in the same way one artist working on different systems will tend to produce different styles using the same artistic vision.  Thus Dietrich's work is made less restricting in terms of personal style but more powerfully expansive by the varying media he chooses.

However, versatility does not always depend on using different kinds of hardware.  Joanne Culver's Frozen Sun Cones is produced using ZGRASS as is Dietrich's Snake 1982 but the two have no obvious visual similarity.  Other artists using the same system, such as Copper Giloth, one of the leading exponents of computer art, show a range of creative expression that is entirely her own.  One example of the use of ZGRASS is the extremely witty film Nuke the Duke, which uses only simple video game graphics.  It was made by Charles Kesler and Jaap Postma of East Carolina University and uses the visual imagery of the amusement arcade.  Its subject is the effect of nuclear radiation which may have caused John Wayne ('the Duke') to die of cancer but despite the serious subject, the film has style, zest and engaging humour.

If sharing a common computer language is unusual among artists there is nevertheless a common interest in types of presentation such as multiple images, animation, and interactive art, in which the viewer affects some aspects of the work displayed.  Interactive art enables the viewer to explore the range of an artist's vision through the ways the pictures can be changed, and also to recognise the formal structure of a piece by noticing what cannot change.  With the advent of interactive videodisks, this kind of art need no longer be restricted to galleries, although the resolution on domestic television sets remains a problem for fast-moving detail.

9897:
There are actually surprising inaccuracies in the article. For instance, the
RCA Studio was released in 1977, the year AFTER the Fairchild VES, which was
the first true programmable videogame system (and in the comment below, the
IBM PC was released in 1981 and the C-64 in 1982). The sweeping statements
are equally awful, i.e., "Everyone in the industry could see that hardwired
games
were a dead end." That's why increasingly sophisticated home Pong-style
systems were made into the late 1970's, right?

Anyway, as for the "game changing" aspect of the Astrocade, conceptually
yes, it was possible, but in practice, probably not. Historically, people
have wanted a dedicated console OR computer, not a console that could also
work as a computer. It's NEVER been particularly successful, be it the APF
M1000 becoming the Imagination Machine, the Mattel Intellivision expanding
first with the Keyboard Component then the ECS, the Creativision, or the
Coleco ColecoVision becoming the Adam, among others. Upon release, the
Astrocade was neither equipped to compete with computers of the day because
of interface issues (the average user wouldn't have found the calculator
keypad particularly inviting) or consoles of the day because of lack of
software.

I suspect if the Astrocade could have been released in quantity in 1977
rather than 1978, it might have had a greater chance of catching on as a
console and use its ability to become a computer as an effective bullet
point against all the other industry players that were either promising or
would eventually promise it. As a games console, the core technology was
certainly competitive and would remain so right up until 1982 with the
release of the ColecoVision.

9904:
There is only one address that ALL extended BASIC's have a problem with. That's
when you go from 32767 to -32767 or !8000. they can't go across that boundary in
a loop. You must go to !7FFF, and then go from !8000 on up. Then you can go to
!FFFF, if you want to. But watch out above !C000, you'll be checking ROM, CART,
and SCREEN. (That's the "floating Memory" of the Lil' WHITE RAM.)

Making a machine language program to test memory is better. It doesn't have the
barrier, and works more thoroughly. If you want, I could make an interactive
memory tester, as could Mike Garber and Rich Degler.
Let us know. I could be done in a short time. (A little longer for me) But there
are several tests that can be done to thoroughly test each memory location. Like
shift left, shift right, powers of !55 (00-!55-!AA_!FF), bit checks, etc. I
think I can do 12 different tests in a program that could be loaded into screen
ram and you could use ANY BASIC.

It's certainly my view that the Bally Professional Arcade could have made it big, if things had been different.  It had great technology for the day, and talented programmers with some good titles.

If I ever write an alternate history novel about the system, I would definitely choose the launch as the point of divergence.  Bally would dedicate enough resources to the system to find and work out all the technical problems like overheating, and they'd distribute it themselves.  It would launch in time for Christmas 1977, carried by a variety of stores nationwide.  Helped by a large ad campaign, it would be a hot seller for the Christmas season, and would continue moving throughout 1978.

With a large installed base, Bally would release more titles, and third parties would start developing for it, being able to make more technically advanced games than they could for the Atari 2600.  Continuing to devote greater resources to the hot system, Bally pushes out the ZGRASS expansion in time for Christmas 1978.  It turns the system into a full-fledged computer, and for less money than anything else then available.  This also moves a good number of units, both from homes upgrading their game system, and from new purchasers wanting a computer in the home.

If the novel continued, it would have to get even more speculative after this.  So I might as well go big.  As more users and developers flock to the Bally Arcade, Atari is relegated to the bargain video game market.  The Intellivision never takes off, and the Odyssey 2 isn't even released.  Bally exercises a degree of quality control, and while it doesn't have as many releases as Atari, there are more than enough quality titles to satisfy the market.  The video game crash never occurs, and Bally starts to get a foothold in the European and Asian markets.  Nintendo is competitive in Japan, but decides not to take on the Bally juggernaut in North America.

The ZGRASS expansion pushes computer penetration to high levels by the early 1980's, and low-price computers like the Commodore 64 can't compete.  Only power users see the need to own anything but a ZGRASS.  ZGRASS becomes the dominant language for graphics and games programming, and many budding programmers start on Bally BASIC (which supports the ZGRASS keyboard as well as the keypad), and then move on to ZGRASS.  They're supported by a number of large-circulation publications, both official and unofficial.  More advanced games are also available for the expansion, prompting many upgrades.

In 1985, Bally releases the Bally Professional Arcade 2, with a new ZGRASS add-on available at launch.  All of the new ZGRASS units have a built-in modem, and Bally offers a service to download games and exchange programs and messages with friends.  Before long, it offers news, weather, and shopping, and as the system price drops, its reach expands beyond traditional computer users.  By the time the Professional Arcade 3 launches in 1991, 40% of US households are on Ballynet.

Bally spends the next couple of years embroiled in a monopoly investigation by the US government over the closed garden Ballynet system, and eventually are forced to let other companies offer access and services on the network.  In the end, though, this may be a blessing in disguise, as the additional services further fuel Ballynet's worldwide growth, and provide more users for its fledgling social networking site, Ballyspace.

With the worldwide obsession with Ballynet, and the newly open system, even more resources are devoted to technology development, and computations per second per dollar begin doubling about every nine months.  The best engineers flock to Bally, and in 1996 they revolutionize the mobile phone market with Ballymobile, which offers worldwide video calling, 3D gaming, and high-speed wireless Ballynet access.

In 2004, researchers running a cluster of ZGRASS 4's design a bio engineered vaccine which primes the human immune system against most cancers.

In 2010, the Professional Arcade 6 offers full immersion virtual reality gaming.

In 2019, Bally wins FDA approval for Ballybots, nano-robots which can cure virtually any disease and even reverse the aging process itself.

By 2025, people spend the majority of their time in Ballyreality.

By 2030, many people have abandoned biological bodies entirely.

By 2035, sentient Ballybots are seeding the universe with intelligence at nearly the speed of light.

Paul

      There are actually surprising inaccuracies in the article. For instance, the RCA Studio was released in 1977, the year AFTER the Fairchild VES, which was the first true programmable videogame system (and in the comment below, the IBM PC was released in 1981 and the C-64 in 1982). The sweeping statements are equally awful, i.e., "Everyone in the industry could see that hardwired games


were a dead end." That's why increasingly sophisticated home Pong-style systems were made into the late 1970's, right?


Anyway, as for the "game changing" aspect of the Astrocade, conceptually yes, it was possible, but in practice, probably not. Historically, people have wanted a dedicated console OR computer, not a console that could also work as a computer. It's NEVER been particularly successful, be it the APF M1000 becoming the Imagination Machine, the Mattel Intellivision expanding first with the Keyboard Component then the ECS, the Creativision, or the Coleco ColecoVision becoming the Adam, among others. Upon release, the Astrocade was neither equipped to compete with computers of the day because of interface issues (the average user wouldn't
 have found the calculator keypad particularly inviting) or consoles of the day because of lack of software. 


I suspect if the Astrocade could have been released in quantity in 1977 rather than 1978, it might have had a greater chance of catching on as a console and use its ability to become a computer as an effective bullet point against all the other industry players that were either promising or would eventually promise it. As a games console, the core technology was certainly competitive and would remain so right up until 1982 with the release of the ColecoVision.

There are actually surprising inaccuracies in the article. For instance, the RCA Studio was released in 1977, the year AFTER the Fairchild VES, which was the first true programmable videogame system (and in the comment below, the IBM PC was released in 1981 and the C-64 in 1982). The sweeping statements are equally awful, i.e., "Everyone in the industry could see that hardwired games


were a dead end." That's why increasingly sophisticated home Pong-style systems were made into the late 1970's, right?


Anyway, as for the "game changing" aspect of the Astrocade, conceptually yes, it was possible, but in practice, probably not. Historically, people have wanted a dedicated console OR computer, not a console that could also work as a computer. It's NEVER been particularly successful, be it the APF M1000 becoming the Imagination Machine, the Mattel Intellivision expanding first with the Keyboard Component then the ECS, the Creativision, or the Coleco ColecoVision becoming the Adam, among others. Upon release, the Astrocade was neither equipped to compete with computers of the day because of interface issues (the average user wouldn't
have found the calculator keypad particularly inviting) or consoles of the day because of lack of software.


I suspect if the Astrocade could have been released in quantity in 1977 rather than 1978, it might have had a greater chance of catching on as a console and use its ability to become a computer as an effective bullet point against all the other industry players that were either promising or would eventually promise it. As a games console, the core technology was certainly competitive and would remain so right up until 1982 with the release of the ColecoVision.

By Charles J. Sippl and Roger J. Sippl
Copyright 1978


A book on how to use programmable calculators seems like an odd place to find references to the Bally Professional Arcade, but it doesn't seem too strange when you remember that the BPA does include a calculator.  This huge 526-page book covers all ranges of calculators and explains that eventually the home computer, such as the Bally, among many others, will be taking the calculators place.


Excerpt from Page xxiii (See book for artwork that accompanies this page)

CALCULATOR INCLUDED IN BALLY VIDEO GAME - CASSETTES INCLUDE MATH EDUCATION AND ART ...

     The Bally Professional Arcade has commercial arcade excitement and fun, and that all begins with Professional-arcade games.  The computer-like console comes with the popular Checkmate, Gunfight games and a sophisticated 4-function, 10-memory printing calculator built in.  The Bally Professional Arcade works for its owner as well as entertains him.  It's a sophisticated 4-function, 10-memory printing calculator with scroll button and entry correction, capable of reconciling bank balances, computing taxes and the like.


Excerpt from Page 45

     Names such as Bally, Ramtek, Micro Inc. and others were certain to become household words as the competition expands.  Microprocessors are again, like they are in advanced programmable calculators, the magic since they permit game controls to be programmed and reprogrammed quickly when developing the original game concept; when offering multiple options for the user, and when building in more features for use with cartridges and tapes.  Such expandable capability allows some of the suppliers to program into home games the ability to make the better games progressively more difficult as the players become more accustomed to the variable formats.  This adaptability heightens the players interest longer and increases his challenge - not only to the games but also to the tools and digital products, very similar in operation and control, to these he uses at work - programmable calculators.


Excerpt from Page 242

     Nearly all microprocessor families can be purchased mounted on chips or boards interfaced easily to peripheral and memory boards and usable with standard programs and code conversions through ROM or other easily programmed media.  The video games by Bally, RCA, Fairchild, National Semi-conductor and others are often advertised as computers because they have a computer-like memory.  Thus, with the home TV as an output device, the games' calculator-type terminals as input devices, and the microprocessors in the games for control, selection, decision-making, and calculating, the game-type home computer will back into personal use rapidly.  And, once used as a computer people will want more versatility.  Many feel the home computer will then come to affect us more drastically than television did; the possible applications are unlimited.  Scores of brands are available, a dozen or more personal computer periodicals have subscriber totals reaching from 35,000 to well over 100,000.  Although this is a calculator book, intelligent readers will desire to be aware of some of the latest microcomputer products, and in a limited space, we shall discuss four models as being representative of the deluge soon to come.
9913:
I made a change to Lance's BIN2BML.  Just a small one.  When you use Astrowav to create a WAV file you are able to set the header and footer lengths to anything that you want.  I thought that perhaps the header of the files that won't load on the Lil' White Ram should be set to 3 seconds (as the default is just 1 second).  I also wanted to change the footer to 1 second.  The way to do this is:

astrowav -h3 -f1 -w<PROGRAM.WAV> <PROGRAM.BIN>

As I've discovered, this does NOT work with BML files.  This only works with BIN files.  However, all is not lost, as the header and footer length can be added or changed in the BML file itself.  I changed Lance's PERL program, BIN2BML, to do this automatically.  I changed this line:

$Out .=" <LOAD format=1 loadNumber=1 checkSum=0xnn>\n";

to this:

$Out .=" <LOAD format=1 loadNumber=1 headerLength=3 footerLength=1 checkSum=0xnn>\n";

Now when using Astrowav to create a WAV file to be loaded via the AstroBASIC interface, the file has a 3 second header and a 1 second footer when using this command:

astrowav <PROGRAM.BML>

Alas, this didn't solve my loading problem with the Lil' White Ram, but it definitely can avoid problems in the future when loading normal BASIC programs.  My current AstroBASIC cart doesn't seem to mind these 1 second headers... but SOME AstroBASIC carts are not as tolerant as this one and they will refuse to load WAV program files that have headers of shorter than 3 seconds.  Trust me, I learned this the hard way through experience.

I hope that this might help someone in the future.

Lance, do you want to make this a permanent change to your program?

9945:
I don't know if you tried working with it at all, but if I remember right, it is
pretty fast. You could try this once to see if it helps

    push af
    push bc
    push de
    push hl     (save what is needed) It appears that IX an IY are not used for
this command.
loopit:
    ld b, 02
    push bc
     $FF
    SYSUCK SCROLL $31 (odd number means that it will automatically suck up the
registers as needed

                                             from the code following. $30
assumes the registers are pre-loaded upon entry)

    # lines to scroll

    # of bytes on line to scroll
    line increment (?) (Direction?)
    Address of first byte
    pop bc
    djnz loopit
    pop everything back


I don't know if those resisters are "sucked in" in that order, or if they are
reversed. It's been too many years.
This routine is NOT re-entrant. Meaning that you just can't keep calling it. You
must load it each time.
I don't know if it saves # of lines and # of bytes. IF it does, the loop will be
shorter, and thus run faster.

Change:
if (($CharCounter > 0)&&($CharCounter < 15))

to

if (($CharCounter > 0)&&($CharCounter <= 15))

That should fix it.

I'm happy to announce that my code to add RAM expansions has been accepted into MESS.  It works basically the same as before, but uses more of MESS's own functions and macros.  In a way, this makes code easier to write, since some things get taken care of behind the scene.  But there was also more of a learning curve than just using C, which I was already familiar with.  It may be awhile before the next official version gets released.  In the meantime, anyone can compile from the public SVN.  Or if you don't want to compile your own, there are automatically compiled daily builds on this site:

http://bobz38.free.fr/mess_autobuild/index.php

To use this, start the Astrocade in MESS and hit tab to bring up the MESS menu.  Then, go to dip switches to change the system configuration.  There are a number of RAM expansions to choose from, as well as the switch to write protect the RAM (make it treated like ROM).  Once you have the configuration you want, hit F3 to do a soft reset.  You can change the RAM write protect switch at any time, but you should always do a reset after changing the RAM expansion.  If you start a cart with a RAM expansion already saved in your configuration file, or switch to a different cart, you may also need to do a soft reset (as with ICBM Attack) to get the cart to start.

This allows you to run extended BASIC carts, and set and read any memory area in the RAM expansion.  You can also set and read the extended memory area addressable by Bally BASIC and AstroBASIC.  I have not, at this time, attempted to add the INS8154 chip to the Blue RAM expansion.  I also have not added the 2K/6K switch.  I'd need tape loading support to test it practically.  Perhaps the next thing to look at is fixing cartridge swapping, which would allow BASICarts requiring a RAM expansion to run in MESS.

It's only when certain things change in a driver that old save states stop working.  For instance, if they add a sound processor, the save state will now require data for it.  Sometimes, the changes aren't so obvious to the end user, though.
